content: Flemish silk-weaver lodging at Mistress Ansell's
He asks, carefully, whether the ladies are punished too, and then he leaves the oath to the gentlemen.
He is from Flanders, and on a feast day he takes the heel and does not hurry another man's post.
He will say the measure the rest of the table is thinking, and he keeps his own name.
Shown the three parish marks, he can say them back, and he will not add a fourth.
He is still under his own name. A silkweaver who is English is not yet him, and he cuts the bread smaller anyway.
From this afternoon the house's sentence for him, to anyone who asks, is that he is from Norwich.
He came to church because not coming would be noticed, and if asked he is from Norwich. When the Counter was told at the step he sat in and added nothing he had not heard.
He stayed at the door of the close. Nobody asked him where he is from.
Asked his birth at a church door, he says Norwich, and he goes up to the garret without a word.
He ties a knot that does not slip, and he speaks over it in his own language.
A bad tooth, he says, takes rent of the whole head. The shuttle goes to Norton Folgate on a Monday. He does not turn barber at the board.
He will finish a sound he has not been asked to translate, and he will not put it into English.
He will speak once of the work in his hands, and he will not be asked where the silk was bought.
In the porch, with Spencer going by, he will say Norwich and refuse any other town.
